stem: A 64-year-old with COPD presents with increased dyspnea. On exam: tripod posture, pursed-lip breathing, paradoxical inward movement of the lower rib cage in inspiration, and an I:E of 1:4. Which single finding best indicates impending ventilatory muscle fatigue?
rationale: Paradoxical (abdominal) breathing indicates diaphragmatic fatigue and impending ventilatory failure more than accessory muscle use alone.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: During vocal fremitus assessment the right lower posterior lung field has markedly increased fremitus compared with the contralateral side. Breath sounds are bronchial in that region. Most likely explanation?
rationale: Both increased fremitus and bronchial breath sounds over a peripheral region point to airspace consolidation (e.g., lobar pneumonia).
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: Which bedside sign most reliably separates central (warm) cyanosis from peripheral (cold) cyanosis?
options: Presence on lips and mucous membranes
rationale: Central cyanosis manifests on lips and mucous membranes and reflects ≥5 g/dL deoxygenated Hgb; peripheral cyanosis affects extremities from low flow/vasoconstriction.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: A patient with suspected right mainstem intubation will most likely have which combination?
options: Absent left breath sounds, unequal chest rise, SpO2 drop
Diffuse wheeze bilaterally, hyperresonance, normal SpO2
Coarse crackles right > left, fever, ↑ fremitus
Stridor and hoarse voice with normal symmetric excursion
rationale: Right mainstem intubation produces absent/markedly reduced left breath sounds, asymmetric chest rise, and hypoxemia.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: In a dark‑skinned patient, the best site to assess central cyanosis is:
rationale: Central cyanosis is best assessed at mucous membranes (inner lips, oral mucosa) or conjunctivae across skin tones.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: During chest expansion assessment, you note markedly diminished excursion on the right posterior base with dullness to percussion and decreased breath sounds. Tactile fremitus is decreased. Most consistent with:
options: Right lower lobe atelectasis with patent bronchus
rationale: Pleural effusion causes dullness, decreased breath sounds, and decreased fremitus (fluid dampens transmission) with reduced excursion.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: A trauma patient has subcutaneous emphysema across the anterior neck after a difficult intubation. First priority bedside action?
options: Check ET tube depth and confirm tracheal placement with capnography
rationale: Widespread cervical crepitus after instrumentation raises concern for airway injury or malposition; verify tracheal placement with waveform capnography and depth before other steps.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: Which respiratory pattern best correlates with pontine lesions?
rationale: Apneustic pattern (prolonged inspiratory gasp with inadequate expiration) is classically linked to pontine lesions.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: ABG: pH 7.12, PaCO2 68, HCO3– 22, PaO2 58 on 50% FiO2. What is the primary disorder and next best action?
options: Acute respiratory acidosis; escalate ventilatory support
Mixed metabolic and respiratory alkalosis; reduce minute ventilation
Chronic respiratory acidosis with compensation; observe
rationale: Low pH with high PaCO2 and normal HCO3– indicates an acute respiratory acidosis. Hypoxemia despite FiO2 0.5 warrants ventilatory support escalation.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: A septic patient has pH 7.32, PaCO2 30, HCO3– 15, lactate 6 mmol/L. Describe disorder and compensation status.
options: Primary metabolic acidosis with partial respiratory compensation
Primary respiratory alkalosis with renal compensation
Mixed metabolic acidosis and respiratory acidosis
Normal acid–base with elevated lactate only
rationale: Low HCO3– with low pH indicates metabolic acidosis. Low PaCO2 shows appropriate respiratory compensation (partial if pH remains acidemic).
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: Which change shifts the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to the LEFT, impairing tissue oxygen unloading?
rationale: Left shift (↑ affinity) occurs with alkalemia, hypothermia, hypocapnia, and decreased 2,3‑DPG—reducing O2 unloading to tissues.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: Calculate expected PaCO2 in metabolic acidosis (Winter’s formula) for HCO3– 12 mEq/L.
rationale: Winter’s formula: expected PaCO2 = 1.5×HCO3– + 8 ±2; for 12 → 26–32 mm Hg. Values outside this imply a mixed disorder.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: In COPD with chronic hypercapnia, which target is safest to avoid CO2 narcosis while correcting hypoxemia?
rationale: Titrate oxygen to SpO2 ~88–92% (PaO2 ≈ 55–65) to avoid suppression of hypoxic drive and worsening V/Q in chronic CO2 retainers.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: ABG: pH 7.44, PaCO2 55, HCO3– 36. Interpretation?
options: Mixed metabolic alkalosis and respiratory alkalosis
rationale: Normal pH leaning acid with high PaCO2 and high HCO3– indicates fully compensated chronic respiratory acidosis (renal HCO3– retention).
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: Which technical error most likely causes spuriously LOW PaO2 on ABG?
rationale: Delayed analysis (not chilled) allows ongoing metabolism → ↓ pH, ↓ PaO2, ↑ PaCO2. Air bubbles raise PaO2 and pH.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: A 24‑year‑old with salicylate toxicity shows pH 7.48, PaCO2 22, HCO3– 16. Best description?
options: Mixed primary respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis
rationale: Salicylates cause a classic mixed disorder: respiratory alkalosis (CNS stimulation) plus metabolic acidosis (uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation).
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: Which device provides the most RELIABLE, fixed FiO2 in tachypneic patients with irregular VT?
rationale: Venturi (air‑entrainment) masks deliver a precise FiO2 independent of patient’s minute ventilation—ideal for irregular VT/RR.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: Nonrebreather at 15 L/min delivers an FiO2 CLOSEST to which range under ideal fit?
rationale: Nonrebreather with one‑way valves and reservoir can approach 0.80–1.00, though true 1.0 is rare without a tight seal.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: In hypercapnic respiratory failure from COPD, which is the most appropriate INITIAL device?
rationale: Controlled low FiO2 via Venturi (24–28%) is appropriate initially; titrate to SpO2 88–92% while monitoring CO2.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: High‑flow nasal cannula (HFNC) physiologic benefits include ALL EXCEPT:
options: Guaranteed fixed FiO2 independent of mouth breathing
rationale: HFNC improves oxygenation via high flows (dead‑space washout, mild PEEP, ↓ inspiratory resistance) but FiO2 can be affected by entrainment and mouth leak.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: Which oxygen safety statement is TRUE?
options: Petroleum‑based ointments are safe under masks
Keep source ≥10 feet from open flame
Use household extension cords with concentrators
Smoking is acceptable with nasal cannulas ≤4 L/min
rationale: Fire safety requires distance from flame/heat and avoidance of petroleum products and smoking around oxygen.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: A patient on 70% Venturi mask is transferred to NRB at 15 L/min and becomes drowsy with rising PaCO2. Most likely mechanism?
options: Suppression of hypoxic ventilatory drive and worsened V/Q mismatch
rationale: High FiO2 may worsen V/Q by reversing hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and suppressing hypoxic drive in CO2 retainers, increasing PaCO2.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: For preoxygenation before intubation in severe shunt physiology (ARDS), which approach best maximizes alveolar oxygenation?
options: HFNC plus tight‑fitting NIV/CPAP with PEEP
rationale: Shunt requires alveolar recruitment: CPAP/NIV with PEEP plus HFNC during apneic phase improves preoxygenation vs NRB alone.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: After 24 h at FiO2 1.0 on ventilator, which is the most effective strategy to reduce oxygen toxicity risk while maintaining PaO2 ≥60?
options: Increase FiO2 further to ensure margin
Add PEEP and titrate FiO2 down
rationale: Use PEEP to maintain oxygenation at a LOWER FiO2 (≤0.6 ideally), reducing oxygen toxicity risk.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: On upright CXR you see a sharp horizontal air–fluid level over the right costophrenic angle with blunting; breath sounds decreased and fremitus decreased. Most likely diagnosis:
rationale: A pleural air–fluid level and blunted costophrenic angle point to pleural effusion; fluid dampens fremitus and breath sounds.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: Which CXR feature favors atelectasis over consolidation?
options: Mediastinal shift TOWARD the opaque side
rationale: Atelectasis often pulls structures toward the affected side (volume loss). Consolidation typically preserves volume.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: Classic progression of ARDS on CXR includes which sequence?
options: Normal → ground‑glass → patchy consolidations → near white‑out
rationale: ARDS evolves from normal/near‑normal to ground‑glass, then patchy dependent consolidations, potentially progressing to diffuse opacification.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: Post‑intubation CXR shows ET tube tip 1 cm above the carina in a patient with planned neck flexion in OR. Best adjustment now?
options: Extubate and reintubate with shorter tube
rationale: Neck flexion advances the ET tube caudally; at only 1 cm above carina, withdraw now to 3–5 cm above to avoid mainstem intubation when flexed.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: A tension pneumothorax is MOST reliably diagnosed bedside by which combination?
options: Absent unilateral breath sounds, hyperresonance, tracheal shift away, hypotension
Diffuse wheeze, prolonged expiratory phase, pulsus paradoxus
Bronchial breath sounds, increased fremitus, egophony
rationale: Classic triad plus hemodynamic compromise strongly suggests tension pneumothorax.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: Capnography during CPR shows PetCO2 rising from 8 → 18 mm Hg with the same compression rate/depth. Interpretation?
options: Improved chest compression quality and perfusion
Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) definitely occurred
rationale: Higher PetCO2 during constant ventilation reflects improved pulmonary blood flow (better compressions). A sudden sustained jump often heralds ROSC.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: Which factor MOST limits the accuracy of pulse oximetry in carbon monoxide poisoning?
options: Overestimation of SaO2 due to carboxyhemoglobin
rationale: Carboxyhemoglobin is read as oxyhemoglobin, falsely elevating SpO2; thus ABG with co‑oximetry is required.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: During V/Q scanning, a normal ventilation with multiple peripheral wedge‑shaped perfusion defects most strongly suggests:
rationale: Mismatch with normal ventilation and segmental perfusion defects is classic for pulmonary emboli.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: On the ventilator: rising peak inspiratory pressure (PIP) with unchanged plateau pressure. Most likely cause?
rationale: ↑PIP with stable plateau isolates the problem to resistive components—airway resistance—rather than compliance.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: Dynamic compliance has fallen substantially while static compliance is unchanged. Which intervention targets the pathophysiology?
rationale: A drop in dynamic (but not static) compliance indicates increased airway resistance; bronchodilators and airway clearance address this.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: Which setting change most effectively reduces ventilator‑induced lung injury in ARDS?
options: Increase VT to 8–10 ml/kg predicted body weight
Set VT 4–6 ml/kg predicted body weight and limit plateau ≤30 cmH2O
rationale: Lung‑protective ventilation with low VT and limited plateau pressure is the cornerstone for ARDS to minimize VILI/overdistension.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: Auto‑PEEP is suspected. Which bedside maneuver confirms dynamic hyperinflation?
rationale: An end‑expiratory hold measures intrinsic PEEP by equilibrating airway pressure at end‑expiration.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: Which change lowers minute ventilation WITHOUT reducing alveolar ventilation in COPD with significant dead space?
options: Increase inspiratory flow to shorten I‑time and allow more expiratory time
rationale: Higher inspiratory flow shortens I‑time, lengthening expiratory time to reduce air trapping while maintaining effective alveolar ventilation.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: During pressure control ventilation, PaCO2 rises despite adequate oxygenation. First-line change?
options: Increase inspiratory pressure (ΔP) or prolong inspiratory time to increase VT
rationale: In PCV, CO2 elimination tracks with delivered VT (and rate). Raising driving pressure or I‑time increases VT and minute ventilation.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: Which bedside indicator most closely reflects increased work of breathing on the ventilator?
options: Rising plateau pressure with constant PIP
Large negative deflections in airway pressure prior to machine breaths
rationale: Large negative swings indicate high patient effort to trigger—suggesting dyssynchrony or inadequate support.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes

stem: In severe shunt physiology, what is the expected response to increasing FiO2 without PEEP?
rationale: True shunt does not improve substantially with FiO2 alone; alveolar recruitment with PEEP is required.
source_refs: Respiratory system advanced content, internal notes
